definition: Generative means having the power to originate, produce, or create something new.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word generative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know generative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The residency proved unexpectedly generative: in ten weeks she drafted two plays and invented a new staging technique.
Productive is weaker than generative: a productive process turns out plenty of output, while a generative one originates genuinely new things.
Seminal is stronger than generative — a seminal work seeds whole fields that grow from it for generations, while generative describes the ongoing power to produce new things at any scale.

Creative means bringing new things into existence, and it usually credits a person's imagination — a creative director, a creative solution. Generative shifts the praise to the source itself: a generative idea, place, or practice keeps producing new things beyond its maker's plans.

Fertile means rich in the power to produce new growth, a soil metaphor: a fertile mind or field is full of latent possibility. Generative is that power caught in the act — actually originating new things, one after another, rather than merely being capable of them.

The city's 'broken block' had been studied for decades with nothing to show.
Then a librarian began hosting open repair nights in the empty storefront.
Within a year, the repair nights had spawned a tool library, the tool library a bicycle co-op, and the co-op a youth apprenticeship that redesigned the block's own lighting.
Planners started calling the storefront the district's most generative square meter — not because of what it contained, but because of what it kept bringing into being.
One repair night keeps originating new things — a tool library, a co-op, an apprenticeship — and that power to bring new things into being is what generative means.

When the music department wheeled a battered modular synthesizer into the lobby, the plan was modest: let students press a few keys between classes.
Instead the machine proved unexpectedly generative.
Students kept wiring it into instruments no manual had described, and each strange new patch inspired the next.
Within two terms the lobby experiments had grown into a student-run workshop, a listening night, and a small festival of homemade electronics.
The synthesizer never got better at making sound; what it kept making was makers.
